overview: Digital Realty Trust is the largest global provider of data center, colocation and interconnection solutions, operating through its PlatformDIGITAL® platform across a portfolio of 310+ data centers (including investments in unconsolidated entities) in 55+ metropolitan areas across more than 30 countries on six continents, representing roughly 2.9 gigawatts of total in-place IT capacity. Digital Realty Trust, Inc. is a Maryland REIT that conducts substantially all of its business through Digital Realty Trust, L.P. (its ~98%-owned operating partnership), leasing wholesale and retail data center space, power and interconnection (cross-connects) to a globally diversified base of more than 5,000 enterprise, cloud, network and content-provider customers under long-duration leases. The company earns essentially all of its revenue from real estate rental and ancillary fee income rather than product sales, making it a capital-intensive, debt-and-equity-funded developer/landlord of mission-critical digital infrastructure rather than an operating technology company.

business_model.summary: DLR leases data center space, power, cooling and interconnection capacity to customers under multi-year contracts (averaging roughly 4 years remaining term, with large >1MW hyperscale deals running 5-15+ years), funding growth through a mix of retained cash flow, equity issuances (ATM program), unsecured bonds in multiple currencies, joint ventures/funds (e.g., the Digital Realty DC Partners NA Fund, Blackstone and Mitsubishi joint ventures) and selective non-core asset sales/contributions. As a REIT, it must distribute at least 90% of taxable income as dividends, so growth capital comes predominantly from external capital markets rather than retained earnings. Revenue is overwhelmingly rental/recurring in nature (long leases with contractual escalators and, for Turn-Key Flex, expense pass-throughs), supplemented by a fast-growing but smaller fee income and other line (construction/development fees and, episodically, large promote income from fund performance hurdles, e.g., ~$201 million of promote income in the nine months ended September 30, 2026 tied to the June 2026 Blackstone-related acquisition).

revenue_streams.name: Rental and other services (stabilized portfolio)
revenue_streams.description: $3,857.8m in the nine months ended September 30, 2026 (+9.0% YoY), from the mature, largely leased-up portfolio; growth driven by new leasing, renewals and utility cost reimbursements

revenue_streams.name: Rental and other services (non-stabilized portfolio)
revenue_streams.description: $1,244.1m in the nine months ended September 30, 2026 (+48.2% YoY), from recently developed, acquired or lease-up assets, concentrated in Northern Virginia, Frankfurt, Paris and Johannesburg

revenue_streams.name: Fee income and other (incl. development fees and promote income)
revenue_streams.description: $359.7m in the nine months ended September 30, 2026 (+268% YoY), boosted by construction/development fees and a one-time ~$201m promote from the June 2026 acquisition; this line can swing sharply quarter to quarter

business_model.customer_type: B2B/enterprise — cloud and IT service providers (e.g., major hyperscalers, IBM, Oracle), content/digital-economy and financial companies (e.g., Meta, LinkedIn, JPMorgan Chase) and network/mobile service providers (e.g., AT&T, Comcast, Lumen, Zayo); more than 5,000 customers in total, with the single largest customer at ~11.7% and the top three customers at ~26% of annualized recurring revenue as of year-end 2025
business_model.geographic_mix: By IT capacity (White Space, as of Sept 30, 2026): Americas ~57% (1,453 MW), EMEA ~34% (870 MW), APAC ~9% (232 MW); by revenue, U.S. ~54% / non-U.S. ~46% of the nine-months-2026 total; by annualized rent concentration, Northern Virginia alone is ~22.6% (the single largest metro), followed by Chicago, Frankfurt, Singapore, London, Amsterdam, Dallas, New York and Paris

main_competitors: regional/private colocation operators in Europe, Asia, Latin America, Africa and Australia
hyperscalers (AWS, Microsoft Azure, Google Cloud, Meta) self-building/self-operating data centers rather than leasing
competitive_position.market_position: Largest global cloud- and carrier-neutral data center, colocation and interconnection platform by footprint and scale (310+ facilities, 55+ metros, 30+ countries), roughly comparable in scale to Equinix but skewed more toward large wholesale/hyperscale deployments versus Equinix's retail/interconnection-dense strength; still a relatively small share of the overall multi-hundred-billion-dollar global data center capacity market, most of which remains self-built by hyperscalers or held by private operators

moat_factors.description: 300+ data centers across 55+ metros on six continents, built since the 2004 IPO through ~$81 billion of cumulative capital raised, would take competitors many years and enormous capital to replicate, particularly given current power and construction-material scarcity

232,000+ cross-connects and ServiceFabric® virtual connectivity to 305+ cloud on-ramps create organically formed, difficult-to-replicate 'connected communities' that attract magnet customers, which in turn attract more customers to the same campuses

8+ gigawatts of future development capacity (including 1,000+ MW developable in Northern Virginia and the new ~1,440-acre Astra Enterprise Park near Kansas City) secured in advance of need, positioned in power-constrained metros where new entrants increasingly cannot find comparable sites or utility capacity

Multi-currency bond access (USD, EUR, CHF, JPY) and a $7.5 billion ATM equity program let DLR fund a capital-intensive growth pipeline that many private or smaller competitors cannot match, though this advantage is itself a function of (and vulnerable to) credit-rating and interest-rate conditions

moat_factors.factor: Long-term contracts with escalators and pass-throughs
moat_factors.description: Leases (especially >1MW hyperscale deals) run 5-15+ years with annual rent escalations and, for most products, utility and tax pass-throughs, giving revenue a REIT-like recurring/visible quality and partially insulating NOI from inflation and power-cost volatility

Customer-installed tenant improvements, physical interconnection relationships and the operational risk/cost of relocating mission-critical infrastructure discourage customer churn, though large hyperscale customers retain the option to build their own facilities over time

weaknesses: High customer concentration at the top end (top 3 customers ~26% of ARR; 20 of 310 data centers are single-tenant) creates event risk if any major hyperscaler slows leasing, renegotiates, or in-sources

Growth is structurally dependent on continuous external capital (equity dilution via ATM issuance, ~9% YoY diluted share growth in 2026, plus ongoing bond issuance) because the REIT payout requirement prevents retaining earnings to self-fund development

Power availability, not demand, increasingly caps how fast DLR (and the industry) can bring new capacity online, meaning revenue growth can lag booked/leased demand by 1-3+ years as projects await utility interconnection
Secondary to Equinix in dense retail/interconnection-heavy markets and in AI-inference workloads that favor smaller, lower-latency sites close to population centers, per some sell-side commentary

Exposure to hyperscaler self-build: AWS, Microsoft, Google and Meta all operate substantial owned data center capacity and could choose to build rather than lease in markets where DLR currently competes

growth_drivers: AI/hyperscale demand supercycle: record quarterly leasing bookings ($626.6 million at DLR's share in Q3 2026) and a record backlog of signed-but-not-commenced leases (reported around $2.5 billion, with roughly $1.4-1.9 billion at DLR's share by various measures), including a 200+ MW AI-inference-oriented hyperscale lease signed in Charlotte in Q1 2026
Development pipeline acceleration: 1,464 MW of projects underway as of September 30, 2026 (a ~90% increase from year-end 2025), 63% pre-leased, at an estimated ~11.6% pre-tax stabilized cash yield

Large land bank for future growth: 8+ gigawatts of future development capacity, including 1,000+ MW developable in Northern Virginia and a new ~600 MW-capable, ~1,440-acre Astra Enterprise Park campus acquired near Kansas City in April 2026 for $482 million

Interconnection/ServiceFabric® growth as customers increasingly deploy multi-region, hybrid-cloud architectures, driving higher-margin cross-connect and connectivity revenue alongside core space/power leasing

Inorganic growth via M&A and capital partnerships: June 2026 acquisition of the remaining ~64% partnership interests in the Digital Carver Dulles 9 and Digital Carver Brickyard joint ventures (~$3.5 billion, including $1.2 billion cash and ~12.3 million DLR shares); the Columbia Capital acquisition (~$690 million, largely in stock, tied to the long-standing Teraco Africa partnership); and continued use of the Digital Realty DC Partners NA Fund (which raised $3+ billion of equity commitments supporting ~$10 billion of data center investment) to recycle capital into new development

Occupancy improvement and lease-up of recently delivered, non-stabilized capacity: consolidated portfolio occupancy rose to 90.7% as of September 30, 2026 from 89.3% at year-end 2025, with total White Space IT Load growing to 2,555 MW

Geographic/product expansion into new metros (e.g., Sofia, Milan, Cyberjaya, Marseille acquisitions in 2026) and continued build-out in power-constrained but high-demand hubs (Northern Virginia, Frankfurt, Paris, Johannesburg)

Secular tailwinds from enterprise data growth ('Data Gravity'), cloud/hybrid-cloud adoption, and artificial intelligence workloads driving sustained, multi-year demand for data center space, power and connectivity

business.description: Top 3 customers represent ~26% of annualized recurring revenue and 20 of 310 data centers are single-tenant; loss, bankruptcy, downsizing or in-sourcing by a major hyperscaler customer could materially impact revenue

Competes against Equinix, NTT, Global Switch, regional operators and increasingly against hyperscalers building and operating their own data centers, which could reduce demand for DLR's newly developed capacity or pressure pricing

Growth is explicitly gated by third-party utility power delivery timelines; DLR's own disclosure flags that aggregate contractual power/cooling obligations could at points exceed physical site capacity, and industry-wide commentary describes power, not demand, as the binding constraint on new supply

Rapid advances in AI compute density, cooling requirements and hyperscaler infrastructure preferences could render existing tenant improvements or facility designs less competitive, requiring costly retrofits
1,464 MW under construction (63% pre-leased) carries budget-overrun, delay and lease-up risk; speculative (non-pre-leased) development could sit vacant if demand softens

financial.description: Total consolidated indebtedness of approximately $19.6 billion as of September 30, 2026 (debt/total enterprise value ~22.4%, effective interest rate ~3.07%); refinancing risk exists if rates or credit spreads rise at future maturities

Generated ~$2.9 billion in net ATM equity proceeds in the first nine months of 2026 alone (new $7.5 billion ATM program established May 2026); diluted Core FFO share count grew roughly 9% YoY, which can mute per-share growth even as aggregate FFO rises
Required to distribute at least 90% of taxable income annually, limiting retained capital and making growth structurally dependent on debt and equity capital markets

Roughly 46% of revenue is generated outside the U.S. (EUR, GBP, CHF, JPY, ZAR and other currencies), creating translation and transaction exposure only partially mitigated by local-currency debt and hedges

regulatory.description: Failure to maintain REIT status for Digital Realty Trust, Inc. or partnership status for the Operating Partnership would have significant adverse tax consequences

Evolving U.S. federal/state and EU energy, carbon and data-center-specific regulations (and related permitting/entitlement processes) could raise costs or delay development; DLR's largest operating expense (utilities) is substantially but not entirely pass-through

DLR cooperated with an SEC Division of Enforcement investigation into the adequacy of its cybersecurity risk disclosures and controls; by letter dated December 22, 2025 the SEC concluded the investigation and did not recommend an enforcement action
Operating 310+ properties across 30+ countries exposes DLR to varied, evolving local permitting, labor, tax and data-privacy regimes (e.g., GDPR), increasing compliance complexity and cost

macro.description: As a capital-intensive, debt-funded REIT, DLR's cost of capital, valuation multiple and development economics are highly sensitive to interest rate levels; ~11% of debt remains unhedged variable rate

macro.risk: AI capex cyclicality / hyperscaler spending pause
macro.description: A significant portion of current record leasing and backlog is tied to AI-driven hyperscaler capital spending; a pause or material cut in hyperscaler capex (a frequently cited tail risk by sell-side analysts) could slow future bookings even though existing long-term leases would likely remain in force

Electricity is DLR's largest operating expense category; while mostly passed through to customers, sustained spikes in power prices, grid instability, or renewable energy certificate costs under existing power purchase agreements could pressure margins and competitiveness in affected markets
Tariffs, supply chain constraints and general inflation can raise construction and operating costs; guaranteed maximum price contracts and rent escalators only partially offset this risk

Community opposition to new data center construction (land use, water/power consumption) can delay permitting in some metros, though this also reinforces pricing power for incumbents with existing entitlements, per industry commentary

macro_factors.industry_outlook: The global data center industry is in the midst of an AI- and cloud-driven supercycle, with record leasing, near-record-low vacancy and rental rate increases across major metros, constrained more by available power than by demand; CBRE and other commentators describe the North American market as power-capacity-limited even amid record construction activity. Multiple sell-side analysts (Green Street, Mizuho and others) remain bullish on large-scale, well-capitalized incumbents like DLR and Equinix, viewing their land banks and ability to shift among markets as durable advantages, while flagging an eventual AI capex slowdown as the primary cyclical risk.
macro_factors.cyclicality: Moderate and increasingly tied to the technology capex cycle (particularly hyperscaler/AI infrastructure spending) rather than traditional real estate cycles; long lease durations (average ~4 years remaining, with large deals running far longer) smooth near-term revenue even if new bookings slow
macro_factors.interest_rate_sensitivity: High — as a REIT reliant on debt and equity capital markets to fund a multi-billion-dollar annual development program, DLR's cost of capital, implied cap rate/valuation, and pace of accretive growth are all directly affected by the rate environment
macro_factors.currency_exposure: Material — roughly 46% of revenue originates outside the U.S. (EUR, GBP, CHF, JPY, ZAR, SGD and others); DLR partially hedges via local-currency debt issuance (e.g., 2026 CHF and EUR note offerings) and derivatives
key_input_costs: Electric power/utilities (largest opex category, mostly passed through to customers)
Construction materials and specialized data center equipment (generators, power distribution units, cooling systems)
Skilled construction and data center operations labor
Capital costs (interest rates/credit spreads on debt, cost of equity)
macro_factors.regulatory_environment: Generally stable property-level regulation (ADA, environmental, zoning) but increasing scrutiny around energy use, carbon emissions and local power-grid capacity; also subject to standard REIT tax-qualification rules and periodic SEC disclosure oversight (the recent cybersecurity-disclosure inquiry was closed without enforcement action in December 2025).

recent_developments.event: Reported Q3 2026 results: Core FFO per share excluding net promote of $2.10 (vs. $1.89 in Q3 2025); raised full-year 2026 Core FFO per share (excluding net promote) guidance to $8.30-$8.35 from $8.15-$8.20, and raised revenue (ex. promote income) guidance to $7.050-$7.125 billion and Adjusted EBITDA guidance to $3.800-$3.850 billion; record quarterly leasing bookings of $626.6 million at DLR's share and a record leasing backlog (reported around $2.5 billion of signed-but-not-commenced annualized rent).

Issued CHF 508.4 million-equivalent (~$611 million) of Swiss franc guaranteed notes (2029/2032/2036 tranches) and €1.0 billion (~$1.1 billion) of 5.125% Euro guaranteed notes due 2036 through finance subsidiaries, funding continued development and refinancing needs.

Portfolio White Space IT Load reached 2,555 MW with consolidated occupancy of 90.7% (up from 89.3% at year-end 2025); development pipeline reached 1,464 MW under construction (a ~90% increase from year-end 2025), 63% pre-leased, at an estimated ~11.6% pre-tax stabilized cash yield; total debt approximately $19.6 billion with a 22.4% debt-to-enterprise-value ratio.
Completed approximately $802.8 million of additional acquisitions, primarily land for future development in Charlotte, Chicago and Indianapolis.

Reported Q2 2026 results: Core FFO ex-net promote of $2.13/share; raised FY2026 guidance to $8.15-$8.20 (from a prior lower range); signed two large hyperscale leases worth $410 million of annualized GAAP base rent (100% share); shares rose as much as ~15% on the guidance raise.

Completed acquisition of the remaining ~64% blended partnership interests in the Digital Carver Dulles 9 JV, LLC and Digital Carver Brickyard JV, LLC joint ventures for approximately $3.5 billion (comprising $1.2 billion cash and ~12.3 million shares of Digital Realty common stock); recognized approximately $201 million of promote income in the nine months ended September 30, 2026 tied to performance hurdles on this transaction. Also completed the Columbia Capital Acquisition (aggregate fair value ~$690.1 million: ~2.3 million DLR shares, $17.1 million cash, and contingent stock consideration), an investment manager long affiliated with DLR's Teraco Africa platform.

Established a new $7.5 billion ATM Equity Offering program (replacing the prior $3.0 billion program, of which $569.9 million remained unsold); contributed two development projects to the Digital Realty DC Partners NA Fund for $447 million gross proceeds and an ~$8 million gain.

Operating Partnership acquired ~1,440 acres of development land at Astra Enterprise Park near Kansas City for $482 million ($377.6 million cash plus ~517,475 OP common units), supporting a large future hyperscale campus.

Signed the company's largest-ever single lease, a 200+ MW AI-inference-oriented hyperscale deal in Charlotte; generated net proceeds of approximately $1.3 billion from ATM equity issuance in the period through May 3, 2026.

SEC Division of Enforcement concluded its investigation into the adequacy of DLR's cybersecurity risk disclosures and related controls, informing the company it did not intend to recommend an enforcement action.

items.target: Record backlog (~$2.5 billion signed-but-not-commenced annualized rent cited by some sources; ~$1.4-1.9 billion at DLR's share by other measures)
items.notes: Much of the record bookings and backlog is not expected to convert to recognized revenue/FFO until 2027-2028 given long lease commencement and build-out timelines

guidance.management_commentary: Management has framed 2026 as a record leasing year driven by AI and hyperscale demand, citing record quarterly bookings, a record backlog, and successive guidance raises (from the original 2026 outlook through the Q2 and Q3 updates) as evidence that current demand is outstripping available power-constrained supply across key metros (Northern Virginia, Frankfurt, Paris, Johannesburg, Chicago). Management has also emphasized the deliberate build-out of forward land bank (Astra/Kansas City, Northern Virginia) and continued portfolio optimization (JV buyouts, Columbia Capital, non-core dispositions/contributions to the DC Partners NA Fund) to sustain multi-year growth, while acknowledging that much of the newly booked leasing will not contribute to earnings until 2027 and beyond, and that continued reliance on ATM equity issuance to fund growth will keep per-share FFO growth below aggregate FFO growth in the near term.

bull_case: AI/hyperscale demand is driving record leasing bookings and a record backlog (~$2.5 billion), providing multi-year revenue visibility as this backlog converts to recognized rent through 2027-2028

Unmatched global scale (300+ data centers, 55+ metros, 232,000+ cross-connects) and an 8+ gigawatt forward land bank in power-constrained markets (Northern Virginia, new Kansas City campus) create a difficult-to-replicate moat as power scarcity, not demand, increasingly caps industry-wide new supply
Management has raised Core FFO, revenue and EBITDA guidance in successive quarters through 2026, evidencing positive execution momentum and conservative initial guide-setting

Diversified, investment-grade-rated access to global capital markets (USD, EUR, CHF, JPY bonds plus a $7.5 billion ATM equity program) supports continued, well-funded development even as the industry's capital intensity rises

Sell-side sentiment is broadly constructive (Moderate Buy consensus, multiple 2026 price-target increases from JPMorgan, TD Cowen, HSBC and Evercore ISI), reflecting confidence in the durability of the current leasing cycle
bear_case: Per-share growth is diluted by heavy, continuous ATM equity issuance (~$2.9 billion raised in the first nine months of 2026 alone, diluted share count +~9% YoY), meaning aggregate FFO growth materially overstates the per-share investor experience

Substantial leverage (~$19.6 billion total debt) and the REIT's 90% payout requirement leave DLR structurally dependent on debt and equity markets to fund growth, creating refinancing and cost-of-capital risk if rates stay elevated or credit conditions tighten

Power availability, not customer demand, is the binding constraint on new supply across the industry; delays in utility interconnection or grid capacity could push out the 1,464 MW development pipeline and the conversion of record bookings into revenue

A material pause or reduction in hyperscaler AI capital spending — a frequently cited tail risk across the sector — could slow future leasing and bookings growth even though existing long-term leases provide some downside protection

Customer concentration (top 3 customers ~26% of ARR) and the long-run possibility that large hyperscalers increasingly self-build rather than lease data center capacity represent structural risks to DLR's addressable market

Much of the 2026 leasing/backlog narrative will not show up in reported earnings until 2027-2028, creating a gap between headline bookings momentum and near-term per-share Core FFO growth that could disappoint if conversion timelines slip
